tepid

TEP-id -- from Latin tepidus, 'lukewarm,' rooted in tepere, 'to be warm.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tepid is only slightly warm; lacking enthusiasm or energy.

Ticket sales stayed tepid throughout opening week, despite the studio's massive advertising budget.

Example

Guests gave the mayor's re-election announcement a tepid round of applause that trailed off within seconds.

The applause was neither excited nor absent -- just weak and half-hearted -- which is exactly the lukewarm, unenthusiastic reaction tepid describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lukewarm: Lukewarm means only slightly warm, and it is the everyday word for it — lukewarm bathwater, a lukewarm review. Tepid means the same thing but sounds more pointed and critical; a writer calls support tepid to stress just how disappointing it is.

unenthusiastic: Unenthusiastic plainly says that a person's excitement is missing, and it points at people and their attitudes. Tepid describes the response itself — the applause, the review, the sales — and tepid can also describe an actual liquid's temperature, which unenthusiastic never can.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fervent: having or displaying passionate intensity

scalding: extremely hot

Where it sits · how little interest it shows

muted → tepid → uninterested

muted vs. tepid: Muted is milder than tepid: a muted response is simply quieter than usual — the interest may still be there, just turned down — while a tepid response has lost the warmth itself.

uninterested vs. tepid: Uninterested is stronger than tepid: a tepid audience still claps a little, without warmth, but an uninterested audience has stopped paying attention altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — tep-: to be warm (Latin (tepere))

suffix — -id: having the quality of (as in vivid, humid) (Latin)

Put it together: Latin tepere meant 'to be warm,' and -id means 'having the quality of,' as in vivid and humid -- so tepid is literally 'having a bit of warmth': lukewarm, and figuratively neither excited nor indifferent.

Use the root in a new word: tepidarium: On the museum's floor plan of the Roman baths, Lena hunted for the tepidarium first.

Root Check

Word Choice

Tepid can describe literal lukewarm liquids, but it's just as often used figuratively for a weak, unenthusiastic reaction -- applause, reviews, or support that falls well short of genuine excitement.
